name: 'Are'are
confidence_why: Naitoro's 2013 first-hand sketch grammar of the middle Malaita dialect gives non-phonemic penultimate stress that shifts to a final or antepenultimate long vowel, with transcribed examples, and the only dissent is Ivens's hedged 1929 remark, without examples, that in the Marau Sound variety on Guadalcanal "the accent, if any, falls on the last syllable"; Geerts 1970, Tryon and Hackman 1983 and Naitoro 2019 say nothing about placement.
catalog_citation: Naitoro, Katerina. 2013. A sketch grammar of 'Are'are: The sound system and morpho-syntax. MA thesis, University of Canterbury. 274 pp. DOI 10.26021/5071; handle 10092/8085 (open CORE mirrorhttps://core.ac.uk/download/35469715.pdf).
catalog_quote: Stress is not phonemic in 'Are'are. Lexical stress normally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word and phrasal stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase: /'ɾo.to/ 'swim' /ɾo.'to.ha/ 'swimming' /'ma.ne/ 'man' /ma.ne.'ne.na/ 'that man' However there are exceptions. If the final syllable contains a long vowel, it will be stressed: /'ha.na/ 'eat' /ha.'ɾaː/ 'wash' If the antepenultimate syllable contains a long vowel it will be stressed: /'aː.wa.ɾa/ 'ten' /'oː.hi.ja/ 'cradle (baby)' In a disyllabic lexeme or phrase where both syllables contain long vowels or diphthongs, the penultimate syllable is stressed. /'a:.tei/ 'who' /'ɾaː..mai/ 'come' The following lexeme seems to be an exception, with the stress falling on the ultimate syllable: /i:.'ta:/ 'what' Function (grammatical) words are normally unstressed. Commonly, vowels in monosyllabic function words are deleted, especially if they are high vowels. In the phrases below, primary stress is shown in the phonetic transcription: ta'aa ni mane /taʔa:ni mane/ [taʔa:n 'mane] 'the males' roto na 'ai /ɾotona ʔai/ [ɾoton 'ʔai] 'fruit of a tree' so'o-na /soʔona/ ['soʔon] 'after, about'

new_statements.rule_in_words: Default stress on the penultimate syllable of the word (and of the phrase), but a long vowel elsewhere attracts stress: a final long vowel is stressed (ha.'raː 'wash'), an antepenultimate long vowel is stressed ('aː.wa.ra 'ten'); when both syllables of a disyllable are heavy (long vowel or diphthong) the penult wins. Stress is not contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; only 'primary stress' is marked in the phonetic transcriptions (p. 24).
new_statements.exceptions: /iː.'taː/ 'what' has final stress although both syllables are long ('seems to be an exception', p. 24). Function (grammatical) words are normally unstressed and their vowels, especially high vowels, are commonly deleted (pp. 24, 30-31).
new_statements.domain_note: Both word and phrase: lexical stress on the penult of the word, phrasal stress on the penult of the phrase (e.g. [taʔaːn 'mane] 'the males'). Based on the 'middle' dialect (Ta'arutona to Rohinari), main consultant and fieldwork in Hauporo, West 'Are'are; auditory analysis, no instrumental study.
new_statements.identity_note: Naitoro 2013 describes the 'middle' dialect of 'Are'are (Ta'arutona to Rohinari; consultants from Hauporo, West 'Are'are), the language-level languoid area1240; Glottolog lists no dialect glottocodes. Ivens 1929/1932 (not opened) describe the Marau Sound emigrant dialect on Guadalcanal, which Tryon & Hackman 1983 treat as one of seven 'Are'are dialects. Geerts 1970 is based on the Tarapaina (Small Malaita Passage) variety.

new_statements.quote: The speech of the people is a difficult one owing to the uncertainty of some of the sounds, to the free interchange of l and r in words, and above all to the way in which the people speak. There is no movement of the upper lip in speaking, the lips are but slightly parted, and the speech is thrust forward as it were. Little stress is put on the words, and the result is a running sound of words, making it very difficult to distinguish between individual words and to catch what is said. There is but little rise and fall of sound. The accent, if any, falls on the last syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Contradicts the catalog's existing statement (Naitoro 2013, pp. 23-24: stress non-phonemic, normally penultimate, final only when the final syllable has a long vowel, antepenult when it has a long vowel — weight-sensitive). new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is weak ('little stress is put on the words', 'little rise and fall of sound'); to the extent there is an accent at all, it falls on the final syllable. An impressionistic 1929 remark, hedged with 'if any', on the Marau Sound variety; no examples or transcriptions marked for stress. Same page also notes contrastive vowel length ('There are both long and short sounds of the vowels, and the doubling of a vowel.. denotes a lengthening of its sound; raa "to go, to come"') and 'There are no closed syllables.'
new_statements.exceptions: none; the hedge 'if any' is the only qualification
new_statements.identity_note: Ivens 1929 describes the language of Marau Sound, Guadalcanal, spoken by immigrants from the Malaita coast (Waisisi, Uhu); Ivens states it is 'probably a form of the language spoken by the Areare people of the south end of Big Mala' (p. 346), and Tryon & Hackman 1983 index Marau (no. 62, Guadalcanal) as an 'Are'are variety. So work 1 is about a dialect of area1240, not main-island 'Are'are as described by Naitoro 2013 or the 'Are'are of Geerts 1970. Tryon & Hackman 1983 cover 'Are'are (1) and (2) as rows 74-75 of the correspondence tables (Malaita) without any stress note.

readall_conflicts: Ivens 1929 (p. 346), describing the Marau Sound variety of 'Are'are on Guadalcanal, says little stress is put on words and that 'the accent, if any, falls on the last syllable' — a hedged, impressionistic final-accent claim with no examples. The catalog's existing statement, Naitoro 2013 (pp. 23-24), describes non-phonemic stress that is normally penultimate, shifted to a final or antepenultimate syllable containing a long vowel (weight-sensitive), with examples and a note that phrasal stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the phrase. These disagree on placement (final vs penultimate) and on the strength of stress. Naitoro's account is the better-supported one (a full modern description with transcribed data, main-island 'Are'are); Ivens' remark is from a short 1927 stay, concerns the Marau Sound dialect, and is explicitly uncertain ('if any'). Tryon & Hackman 1983 is silent and creates no conflict.

sources.note: Sect. 2.2 'Stress', pp. 23-24: stress not phonemic; lexical stress normally on the penultimate syllable of the word and phrasal stress on the penult of the phrase; a long vowel in the final or antepenultimate syllable attracts stress; if both syllables of a disyllable are long/diphthongal the penult is stressed; /iː.'taː/ 'what' is an exception with final stress; function words are normally unstressed and often lose their vowels.

sources.quote: 4. The accent, if any, falls on the last syllable. There is no movement of the upper lip on the part of the people when speaking, and the speech is thrust forward as it were, the lips being parted but slightly. Little stress is put on the words; there is little rise and fall of sound, and the result is a running and unvaried stream of sound. [...] 6. The letters employed are a, e, h, i, k, l, m, n, o, p, r, s, t, u, w. The vowels have the Italian sounds. The doubling of a vowel, except where a 'break' occurs, indicates a long vowel sound. No nasal sounds occur in the language.

sources.note: Ivens states a fixed FINAL accent, hedged ('if any'), and describes stress as weak ('little stress is put on the words'), with flat intonation ('little rise and fall of sound'). The catalog entry (Naitoro 2013) codes 'Are'are as weight-sensitive with long-vowel syllables heavy; Ivens gives no weight rule and no secondary stress, and his final-accent statement is a different system statement, so it contradicts the catalog's kind -- but it is a one-sentence impressionistic note from 1927 fieldwork on the Marau Sound (Guadalcanal migrant) variety, not a phonological analysis, and the hedge plus t
